title: Reversible liquid-phase lithium transfer across the battery lifecycle
content: Lithium underpins high-energy-density batteries and has become strategically critical for sustainable energy transitions. Conventional solid lithium sources used in battery manufacturing suffer from poor interfacial contact, heterogeneous lithium delivery and limited diffusion kinetics, constraining production efficiency and material utilisation. Lithium–arene complexes (LACs), formed by the reversible reaction between lithium and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), provide a liquid-phase route for lithium transfer. In this review, we describe the PAH/LAC pair as two chemical states of a reversible lithium carrier, where PAH represents the Li-depleted state and LAC the Li-loaded state. We first discuss the fundamental chemistry of PAH/LAC conversion and the factors determining LAC reduction potential, including PAH structure, solvent environment, temperature and concentration. We then summarise the applications of PAH-based lithium extraction, including lithium-based foil fabrication, lithium-alloy modification and quantitative analysis of inactive lithium, followed by LAC-based lithium donation for anode and cathode pre-lithiation, electrode and cell-level lithium supplementation, spent-cathode regeneration and the synthesis of lithium-containing materials. These processes are further evaluated in terms of reaction time, process efficiency, lithium utilisation, material compatibility and process requirements. Particular attention is given to the recovery and reuse of PAHs and solvents, and to the possibility of transferring lithium recovered from one process directly to another. Finally, we discuss molecular design, process integration and closed-loop lithium transfer as directions towards practical implementation of the PAH/LAC pair across the battery lifecycle.
